tance. The  place  where  he  was  was  thick  with  timber,  there  being  many
young  willow  trees.  Coyote  sat  down  and  wondered  what  he  should  do
to  gain  the  friendship  of  Spider- Woman.  Coyote  took  hold  of  his  mem-
brum  and  began  to  play  with  it.  Soon  it  became  hard  and  he  stuck  it
out  from  the  timber.  He  kept  moving  it  backwards  and  forwards  and

Yonder  I  see  it  with  my  eyes,

Yonder  I  see  it  with  my  eyes.

You,  yonder,  moving  back  and  forth  from  the  bushes,

Ugly  red  thing,    O!

She  continued  to  sing,  and  after  a  while  she  began  to  dance.  Then
Coyote  moved  faster  and  the  old  woman  began  to  sing  and  dance  faster.

went  on  about  his  business.

She  who  was  my  wife.

Old  man's'membrtmi,  crooked

Coyote-Man  on  the  robe.  Then  these  men  carried  Coyote-Man  to  the
lodge.  When  Coyote-Man  was  placed  in  the  lodge  he  took  his  bundle,
put  it  in  the  lodge,  and  said:  "You  people  can  now  go  out  from  the  lodge
and  stay  at  a  distance,  for  I  am  to  wash  this  young  man  and  put  medi-
cine upon  him."  The  people  went  out  and  stood  some  distance  away.
Coyote-Man  took  a  kettle,  placed  it  upon  the  fire,  and  went  and  got  a  piece
of  iron.  This  he  placed  in  the  fire.  Then  he  told  the  wounded  man  to
sit  near  the  fire  and  he  would  wash  his  wound.  The  man  began  to  feel
of  the  wound  and  it  was  almost  healed.  Coyote-Man  took  the  red-hot
iron  from  the  fire,  rammed  it  into  the  side  of  the  young  man,  and  said:
"This  is  the  way  I  doctor  you.  I  will  kill  you  and  that  will  be  the  end  of
you."  He  killed  him,  took  out  his  knife,  and  cut  him  up.  He  cut  the
meat  into  small  slices  and  put  it  in  a  kettle.

After  he  had  eaten  he  saw  a  little  Snake  crawling  up  towards  him,  and
the  Coyote-Man  said:  "My  grandson,  I  will  give  you  something  to  eat."
Coyote-Man  cut  a  strip  of  meat  and  shoved  it  down  into  the  throat  of  the
Snake,  so  that  it  was  nearly  choked  and  could  not  speak.  The  Snake
crawled  out  of  the  lodge  and  went  to  where  the  people  were.  It  was
windy,  so  that  when  the  Snake  tried  to  speak  the  people  could  not  hear  it.
The  Snake  came  close  to  one  person  and  spoke  to  him.  The  Snake  spoke
very  low,  for  it  could  hardly  speak  on  account  of  the  meat  which  was  down
in  its  throat.  The  person  then  said:  "People,  this  Snake  says  something."
They  all  stopped  and  Hstened  and  the  Snake  spoke  again  in  a  whisper  and
said:  "That  man  killed  the  boy  in  the  lodge  some  time  ago,  and  has  eaten
him  up."

The  people  then  ran  to  the  lodge  and  there  they  found  the  bones  of
the  boy  and  some  of  the  meat  still  boiling,  but  the  man  was  gone.  They
hunted  for  him  through  the  timber,  but  they  could  not  find  him.  His
medicine-bag  and  other  things  were  left  in  the  lodge.

Coyote-Man,  after  he  left  the  lodge,  went  through  the  timber,  and  after
a  while  he  went  out  and  began  to  climb  a  hill.  As  he  reached  the  top  of
the  hill  he  saw  several  Buzzards  sitting  upon  the  hill.  Then  he  began  to
talk  to  the  Buzzards  and  they  listened  to  him.  Coyote-Man  asked  the
Buzzards  to  carry  him  up  into  the  sky,  so  that  he  could  look  down  as  they
did  and  see  what  the  earth  was  like.  Two  Buzzards  went  away,  while
two  remained  behind.  The  two  who  remained  behind  told  Coyote-Man
to  put  his  arms  around  their  necks  and  they  would  take  him  up.  When
the  Buzzards  flew  the  Coyote-Man  would  say:  "Grandchildren,  wait,
wait;  I  can  not  stand  this.     You  might  drop  me."

444  COYOTE   TALES.

Several  times  they  flew  with  him,  but  each  time  Coyote-Man  begged
them  to  go  back  to  the  ground.  At  last  the  other  two  Buzzards  told
Coyote-Man  that  he  must  close  his  eyes.  Coyote-Man  closed  his  eyes
and  the  Buzzards  flew  up.  After  they  were  away  up  high  then  they
told  the  Coyote-Man  to  look.  Coyote-Man  looked  down  and  he  could
see  game  upon  the  ground.  Then  he  said:  "My  grandchildren,  if  I  had
power  to  fly  high  I  could  see  where  the  game  is  and  then  go  down  and
kill  it.  I  would  then  have  plenty  to  eat."  The  Buzzards  kept  flying
with  him.  The  other  two  who  had  left  first  were  in  the  lead.  After
a  while  the  two  leading  Buzzards  circled  around.  Then  the  Buzzards
told  him  to  close  his  eyes.  When  the  Buzzards  swung  around  they
came  to  a  certain  place  and  there  the  two  Buzzards  separated,  one  going
one  way  and  the  other  another  way.

Coyote-Man  was  dropped  into  a  hollow  log,  for  the  Buzzards  wanted
to  kill  him.  The  two  who  had  gone  on  ahead  of  the  other  two  found  the
hollow  log.  When  they  found  it  they  brought  the  other  two,  who  were
flying  with  Coyote-Man.  Coyote-Man  remained  in  this  hollow  log  for
several  days.  There  were  holes  in  the  sides  of  the  hollow  log.  Coyote-
Man  began  to  make  them  a  little  larger,  so  that  he  could  look  through
them.  One  day  he  heard  a  great  noise,  as  if  there  were  many  people
traveling.  He  made  a  big  hole.  He  looked  and  saw  many  people
traveling.  They  were  making  their  camp  near  the  log.  After  the  women
had  put  up  their  tipis  they  went  into  the  timber  to  gather  dry  limbs.  When
Coyote-Man  saw  the  women  coming  he  took  his  quiver,  cut  the  raccoon
tails  from  his  quiver,  and  stuck  them  into  the  holes  of  the  log.  When  the
women  came  and  saw  the  raccoon  tails  they  thought  that  they  had  found
a  hollow  log  where  the  raccoons  stayed.  When  the  women  came  to  the  tree
they  saw  the  tails  sticking  out.  They  caught  hold  of  the  tails  and  pulled
them.  Coyote-Man  pulled  inside.  Then  the  women  said:  "Here  are
some  raccoons.  Let  us  cut  the  tree  down  and  get  them  out."  They  cut
the  tree  down,  and  as  it  fell  over  Coyote-Man  stood  up  and  said:  "What
do  you  women  mean  by  cutting  down  my  house.''  This  is  my  house."
He  was  very  angry  with  the  women,  but  at  the  same  time  he  was  thank-
ful that  they  had  cut  down  the  tree."
}

the  Beavers,  and  some  of  them  ran  away  into  the  water.  Coyote  then
went  up  and  brought  his  children  and  they  took  the  Beavers  up  to  their
lodge.  There  they  skinned  them  and  had  plenty  to  eat.  After  they  had

again,  but  the  Beavers  would  not  listen  to  Coyote  any  more.

126.  COYOTE  AND  THE  ROLLING  STONE.'

Coyote  was  going  along,  and  as  he  had  not  had  anything  to  eat  for
some  time  he  was  very  hungry.  In  the  evening  he  went  to  a  high  hill  and
sat  down.  Early  the  next  morning  he  started  again.  He  came  to  a  big
round  stone.  He  took  out  his  knife  and  said:  "Grandfather,  this  knife
I  give  to  you  as  a  present.     I  want  you  to  help  me  to  get  something  to  eat. ' '

Coyote  went  over  a  hill,  and  there  in  the  bottom  was  a  village  of  people.
He  went  into  the  village  and  he  could  see  meat  hanging  on  poles  every-
where in  the  camp.  He  went  into  one  of  the  tipis  and  the  people  in  the
tipi  roasted  a  piece  of  meat  for  him.  Just  as  he  was  about  to  taste  of  the
meat  he  thought  of  his  knife  and  said:  "Why  did  I  give  my  knife  to  that
stone  ?  I  should  have  kept  it  and  then  I  should  have  been  able  to  cut  the
meat  without  having  to  pull  it  with  my  hands."  He  asked  to  be  excused
and  went  out.  He  went  to  where  the  stone  was.  He  said:  "Grandfather,
I  will  have  to  take  back  this  knife,  for  I  have  found  a  village  of  people  with
plenty  of  meat."  He  went  over  the  hills  and  into  the  bottom,  but  there
was  no  village  there.  Coyote  went  back  and  returned  the  knife  to  the
stone.  He  went  back  over  the  hills  and  there  saw  the  village  and  he
entered  one  of  the  tipis.  They  placed  before  him  some  meat.  He  began
to  chew  the  meat.  He  thought  of  his  knife.  He  went  back  to  the  stone,
and  as  he  took  the  knife  the  stone  said:  "Why  do  you  take  the  knife
away  from  me?  I  am  now  going  to  kill  you."  Then  the  stone  ran  after
the  Coyote.  Coyote  ran  and  came  to  a  den  of  Bears.  He  told  the  Bears
that  a  person  was  running  after  him  and  he  asked  them  to  help  him.  The
Bears  said  that  they  were  not  afraid  of  anything.  They  asked  what  the
thing  was,  and  he  said  it  was  the  stone.  The  Bears  said:  "  Keep  on  run-
ning. We  can  not  do  anything  with  the  stone."  The  stone  was  close  to
Coyote  when  he  came  up  to  another  den  of  Mountain-Lions.  They  also
told  Coyote  to  pass  on,  as  they  could  not  do  anything  for  him.  After
awhile  Coyote  came  to  a  Buffalo  standing  all  alone,  but  when  the  Buffalo
found  out  that  it  was  the  stone  running  after  Coyote  he  told  him  to  pass  on.

'  Told  by  Leading-Sun,  Kitkehahki.  The  story  is  told  to  the  children  so  that
when  they  give  presents  to  stones,  trees,  or  any  other  thing  they  must  never  take
them  away  again;  that  if  they  took  away  the  presents  something  would  happen  to
them  and  cause  their  death."

At  last  Coyote  came  to  a  place  where  the  Bull-Bats  stayed.  Coyote

Bats  then  said:  "Enter  our  lodge  and  remain  there."  When  the  stone
came  rolling  up  it  said:  "Where  is  that  person  who  came  here?"  The
Bull-Bats  did  not  reply  and  the  stone  became  angry.  Then  the  Bull-
Bats  said:  "He  is  here  and  we  are  going  to  protect  him."  The  Bull-Bats
flew  up  and  then  down,  and  they  expelled  flatus  on  the  stone.  Every
time  they  did  this  a  piece  broke  off  from  the  stone.  The  largest  Bull-Bat
came  down  and  expelled  flatus  right  on  the  center  and  broke  the  stone
into  pieces.     Then  the  Coyote  was  told  to  come  out  and  go  on  his  way.

Coyote  started  off,  and  when  he  got  over  the  hills  he  turned  around  and
yelled  at  the  Bull-Bats  and  said:  "All  you  big-nosed,  funny  things,  how
you  did  behave  to  that  stone."  The  Bull-Bats  heard  it  and  did  not  pay  any
attention,  but  he  kept  on  making  fun  of  them.  Then  the  Bull-Bats  flew
up  in  a  group,  and  came  down,  and  with  their  wings  they  got  the  stones
together  again  and  started  it  to  rolling,  and  said:  "Go  and  kill  that  fellow."
The  stone  then  ran  after  Coyote  and  Coyote  tried  to  get  away,  but  he
could  not.  At  last  he  gave  out.  He  jumped  over  a  steep  bank  and  the
stone  was  right  behind  him.  As  Coyote  struck  the  bottom,  the  stone  fell
on  him  and  killed  him.  This  is  why  we  used  to  find  dead  coyotes  in  the
hills  and  valleys.

127,  COYOTE  AND  THE    ROLLING  SKULL'

Coyote  was  going  along,  and  he  became  very  hungry.  He  came  to  a
wide  prairie  covered  with  tall  buffalo-grass.     He  stopped  and  sang:

What  a  fine  place  this  is;

I  wish  I  could  run  the  buflfalo  around;

Thus  I  might  get  something  to  eat.

Close  by  where  Coyote  was  singing  a  voice  spoke  and  said:  "Stop
singing  and  dancing  around  my  place."     Then  the  skull  began  to  sing:

Here   my    skull    rests,
Here   my   skull   rests.
Surrounded  by  a  path.
Here  my  skull  rests.

'  Told  by  White-Sun,  Kitkehahki.  This  story  was  originally  told  by  his  grand-
father, one  of  the  leading  medicine-men  of  the  Kjtkehahki.  It  is  told  to  teach  the
children  that  when  they  find  skulls  upon  the  prairie  they  must  not  call  them
names  nor  kick  them  around.  The  children  are  taught  by  the  story  that  skulls  have
supernatural  power.

448  COYOTE   TALES.

Here  my  skull  rests,

But  there  you  stand,  Coyote,

Dying  of  starvation.

Here  my   skull   rests.

Here  my  skull  rests.

But  there  you  stand.  Coyote,

Awaiting  the  odor  of  meat  borne  by  the  wind

Here  my  skull  rests.

Coyote  looked  up  and  said:  "And  who  are  you  that  I  should  be  afraid
of  you?"  Just  then  a  skull  rolled  up,  and  when  Coyote  saw  the  skull  he

last  he  ran  to  a  village  of  people  and  just  as  he  ran  into  the  village  and
called  to  them  the  skull  devoured  him.  The  people  who  ran  out  from  their
village  were  also  devoured  by  the  skull.  Four  girls  escaped  and  started  to
run,  but  the  skull  pursued  them.  When  the  skull  was  about  to  catch  one
of  the  girls,  she  threw  her  pack  strings  upon  the  ground,  and  many  bunches
of  cactus  sprang  up  over  the  land.  The  girls  ran  on,  and  the  skull  tried

it  did  get  over  it  ran  and  killed  the  woman  who  had  thrown  the  pack
strings.  The  second  woman  threw  her  pack  strings  upon  the  ground  and
there  was  a  big  stream  of  water  and  a  steep  bank.  The  skull  could  not
cross  the  stream  of  water,  but  somehow  it  managed  to  jump  upon  logs
which  were  floating  down  and  so  crossed  the  stream.  Then  it  took  after
the  woman  and  killed  her.

When  the  skull  was  about  to  overtake  the  other  two  women,  one  of
them  threw  her  pack  strings  upon  the  ground  and  there  was  a  steep  bank.
But  somehow  the  skull  managed  to  climb  up  and  took  after  the  woman
and  killed  her.  Then  the  fourth  girl,  the  youngest,  ran  and  cried  for  help.
A  Bull-Bat  flew  by  her  and  told  her  to  go  down  into  the  hollow;  that  there
she  would  see  a  man ;  that  he  alone  could  help  her.  The  girl  went  down
into  the  ravine  and  there  she  saw  a  little  lodge  and  a  small  boy,  as  she
thought,  sitting  outside  of  the  lodge.  She  told  him  that  a  skull  was  com-
ing after  her.  He  told  her  to  go  into  his  lodge,  and  he  would  stay  where
he  was.  The  skull  came  and  asked  the  little  fellow  if  a  girl  had  gone  on
by.  He  paid  no  attention  to  the  skull,  and  the  skull  became  angry  and
was  about  to  devour  him,  when  he  opened  his  mouth  and  blew  with  his
breath  a  little  blue  bead.  The  blue  bead  struck  the  skull  upon  the  fore-
head, killing  it.  The  little  fellow  told  the  girl  to  go  on  her  way;  that  the
skull  was  killed  and  would  never  molest  the  people  any  more.  The  little
fellow  was  Milk- Weed  and  the  girl  was  called  Rolling  Skull."

what  a  fat  Turkey!  If  I  had  only  killed  him  instead  of  fooling  my  time
away.  Now  I  have  nothing  for  my  children  to  eat,  for  I  have  let  him
slip  away."  Then  Coyote  hallooed  to  Turkey  and  said:  "Let's  com-
plete the  ceremony;  you  must  not  be  scared;  my  songs  did  not  mean
anything."     But  Turkey  never  came  back.

134.  COYOTE  AND  THE  DANCING  TURKEYS.'

A  bunch  of  Turkeys  were  dancing,  when  Coyote  came  up  to  them.
"Grandchildren,  you  are  not  singing  a  good  song;  I  can  teach  you  a  good
song,"  said  he.  "Very  well,"  all  the  Turkeys  said;  "sing  us  a  good  song."
Coyote  sang:

'Told  by  White-Eagle,  Skidi.  The  story  is  told  to  the  children  so  that  they
might  imitate  the  dancing  of  the  turkeys  and  should  dance  this  dance  when  playing
in  the  night.

458  COYOTE   TALES.

Gizzard!     Gizzard!

Lift  your  necks  high,  then  low,

Waving  your  tails  to  and  fro.

Tut!  Tut!     (Sound  of  turkey  when  jumping.)

As  he  sang  the  song  the  Turkeys  stretched  their  necks  and  placed  them
on  the  ground,  but  they  watched  Coyote,  for  as  he  danced  among  them
he  would  open  his  mouth  as  if  to  bite  their  necks.  The  Turkeys  would
say:  "His  mouth  is  open!  Lookout!"  But  Coyote  sang  louder.  They
danced  and  danced,  and  all  at  once  Coyote  jumped  and  bit  the  necks
of  the  twobiggest  Turkeys  and  killed  them.  The  others  ran  away.  "Ah!"
said  Coyote,  "I  am  quite  a  cheat;  my  children  will  have  plenty  to  eat."

Coyote  took  the  two  Turkeys  home  and  said:  "Children,  pick  the
feathers  off  and  cut  the  meat  off  and  put  it  in  the  pot  and  cook  it.  I  am
going  to  ask  some  of  the  chiefs  to  eat  with  me,  but  I  will  save  some  meat
for  you."  He  went  off,  and  after  he  came  back  he  sent  his  children  and
wife  away.  He  went  into  their  tipi  and  sat  down.  Once  in  a  while  he
would  swing  the  skin  that  hung  over  the  entrance  and  say:  "Nawa,  take
this  seat."  The  children  could  hear  some  one  else  say:  "Nawa,  thanks;"
and  they  thought  that  there  were  many  people.  After  a  while  Coyote
made  a  speech  and  said:  "I  have  two  Turkeys  boiling  and  I  invite  you  to
help  me  eat  them."  He  said  "Nawa"  a  number  of  times;  so  the  little
ones  thought  that  there  were  many  people  in  the  tipi.  Old  Coyote  took
the  kettle  off  and  commenced  to  dish  out  the  meat.  He  went  from  one
plate  to  another  and  ate  all  of  the  meat  by  himself.  One  of  the  children
went  in  and  saw  his  father  eating  by  himself,  and  went  back  and  told  his
mother.  They  all  came  out  and  made  a  rush  into  the  tipi,  and  old
Coyote  ran  away  and  the  children  had  only  bones  to  eat  and  they  were
left  to  hunt  food  for  themselves.

135.  COYOTE  AND  THE  TURKEYS  ROLL  DOWN  THE  HILL'

Coyote  was  going  along  and  he  saw  many  Turkeys  sliding  down  a  hill.
"What  shall  I  do?"  he  said  to  himself.  "I  will  go  back  and  get  a  sack
and  show  these  Turkeys  something  new."  He  got  his  sack  and  went
back  to  where  the  Turkeys  were.  "Now,  my  grandchildren,  I  have  some-
thing new.  Watch  me  go  into  this  sack.  When  I  am  inside  tie  it  fast.
Now  roll  me  down  the  hill."  As  he  rolled  down  the  hill  he  laughed  and
laughed,  and  said:  "It  is  very  fine  to  roll  down  hill."  At  the  foot  of  the
hill  the  Turkeys  untied  the  sack  and  Coyote  walked  up  the  hill  with  them.

'  Told  by  Fox,  Skidi.  The  story  is  to  teach  the  children  that  when  they  grow
up  and  hunt  for  game  and  kill  it  they  should  always  be  sure  to  keep  watch  over  it
and  preserve  it."

the  sack  and  untied  it.  The  Turkeys  were  very  anxious  to  get  out  and
made  a  big  cackling  noise,  scratched  the  young  Coyotes,  and  made  their
escape.  The  young  ones  cried  and  cried.  When  the  old  Coyote  came

Coyotes.  The  little  Coyotes  went  off  crying  and  singing  this  song  about

Thus    father    likes.

When   he  is   scared.

To   lay   back   his   ears.

Ha-o-o,    haho,
Ha-o-o,    haho.

Prairie-Chicken.  He  greeted  Prairie-Chicken  and  said:  "Prairie-Chicken,

Prairie-Chicken  said  that  he   would,  not    suspecting  that    Coyote   was

always  to  be  on  the  look-out  lest  they  be  frightened  by  prairie  chickens  flying  up  in

planning  to  get  a  chance  to  kill  and  eat  him.  They  selected  a  place  where

Chicken  came  along  he  jumped  at  him  and  tried  to  scare  him,  but  Prairie-

gave  a  great  leap,  for  he  was  frightened.  He  jumped  over  the  steep  bank

and  so  met  their  death  through  fear.

Who  now  is  going  to  bewitch  me.

Coyote  sang  again  and  said:

Prairie-Chicken  yonder,  sitting  on  a  limb.
Somebody  is  going  to   bewitch   you.

Then  Prairie-Chicken  asked  in  a  song:

Who  now  is  going  to  bewitch  me.
And  with  what  shall  I  be  poisoned?

ter of  Scabby-Bull,  a  great  medicine-man  among  the  Skidi,  and  who  had  many

All  of  the  things  you  mention

I  am  fond  of;   I  like  to  eat  them.

Then  Prairie-Chicken  flew  up  and  away  and  Coyote  went  his  way
among  the  hills.

138.  COYOTE  TRIES  TO  MARRY  RABBIT.'

Coyote  was  going  along  and  he  met  a  female  Rabbit.  He  tried  to
marry  her,  but  she  would  not  have  him,  and  she  ran  away  from  him.
Then  the  female  Rabbit  went  to  another  Coyote  and  tried  to  marry  him.
The  Coyote  began  to  sing:

Rabbit-Woman,   standing  here,
Rabbit-Woman,  standing  here,
Wants  to  marry  my  son.
But  one  fault  I  find  with  you;
Your  nose,  like  the  earth.
In  many  places  is  cracked.

The  Rabbit  then  said:  "Your  people  and  my  people  shall  always  be
apart  and  never  mix  up."     Then  they  went  off.

'Told  by  Yellow-Calf,  Skidi,  keeper  of  the  Big-Black-Meteoric-Star  bundle.
The  story  is  told  to  teach  the  children  that  the  rabbit-people  and  the  coyote-people
are  two  different  sorts  of  animals.

462  COYOTE    TALES.

139.  COYOTE  AND  THE  SALT.'

A  long  time  ago  the  people  did  not  have  any  salt.  The  people  had
heard  of  Coyote  wandering  over  the  land ;  that  at  one  time  he  turned  into
a  man,  made  a  big  fire  upon  a  high  hill,  and  began  to  roast  some  meat.
Several  of  the  people  went  up  to  where  Coyote-Man  was  and  he  gave
them  pieces  of  roasted  meat  with  salt  on  it.  When  the  people  ate  the
salted  meat  it  tasted  so  good  that  when  they  went  home  they  told  their
children  to  recite:

Coyote    standing    yonder.

Yonder  on  the  hill  by  the  fire.

Give  me  some   salt.

I  am  going  to  eat  soup  from  a  wooden  bowl.

The  children  said  this  many  times  to  the  Coyote-Man,  and  the  Coyote-
Man  finally  promised  the  people  to  lead  them  to  a  place  where  they  could
get  salt.  In  those  times  the  people  did  not  have  any  horses,  so  the  men
and  women  carried  south  their  tipis  and  belongings  upon  their  backs.
Coyote-Man  led  them.  They  found  the  salt  in  the  south.  The  people
dug  the  salt  in  lumps  and  carried  the  lumps  home  with  them.  Coyote-
Man  disappeared  and  was  never  seen  again,  but  after  that,  when  the
children  saw  Coyotes  upon  high  hills,  they  recited  this  Uttle  ritual  to
remind  the  Coyotes  that  they  were  the  ones  who  found  the  salt  for  the
people.

140.   COYOTE  AND  THE  ROSEBUDS.'

The  Coyote  people  went  on  a  buffalo  hunt,  and  as  there  were  no  buf-
falo in  sight  they  sent  scouts  out  over  the  country  every  day  to  look  for
buffalo.  One  day  they  sent  out  several,  and  one  of  them  went  off  by
himself.  He  went  up  on  a  high  hill  and  saw  that  there  were  rosebuds
from  one  end  of  the  valley  to  the  other.  He  sat  on  the  hill  for  a  long

Now  there  must  be  rat  trails  in  the  forest,
Now  there  must  be  rat  trails  in  the  forest,
Made  by  Black  Rats,  made  by  Black  Rats.
The   artichoke   vines  will   climb
Upon  the  red  willows,  and  there
If  you  dig  you  will  find  artichokes.
From  this  time  you  will  find  artichokes
With  eyes  like  an  ash  tree.

Then  Magpie  sang  to  the  White  Rat:

Hunting  ground  beans,  hunting  ground  beans;
That  is  hunting  something,  hunting  something.
Among  the  willows  you  will  find  earth-nuts,
Earth-nuts  by  the  willows  under  the  ground.
You  shall  go  there  to  the  willows;
There  you  will  find  soft,  crumbling  soil.
Hereafter,    White    Rat,
You  shall  live  on  earth-nuts.

Each  of  the  Rats  went  his  way,  singing:  "The  errand  bird  of  the  god
in  the  north,  who  is  known  as  'Ready-to-Give,'  has  given  us  artichokes  to
eat."

Ever  since  that  time  the  White  Rat  has  been  known  as  the  ground-
bean  Rat  and  the  Black  Rat  as  the  artichoke  Rat.

147.  TURTLE'S  WAR  PARTY.'

Turtle  started  on  the  war-path.  On  the  way  he  met  Mosquito.  Mos-
quito asked  Turtle  where  he  was  going  and  Turtle  said:  "We  have  a
root  sticking  into  us  and  we  are  mad.  I  am  on  the  war-path."  Mosquito
then  asked  that  he  be  allowed  to  join,  and  the  Turtle  said:  "All  right."
After  a  while  Cricket  met  the  war  party  and  asked  that  he  be  allowed  to
join,  and  they  consented.  The  three  warriors  traveled  on  until  they
came  to  a  lodge.  They  entered  the  lodge  and  tried  to  kill  the  people  who
were  inside,  but  they  were  discovered.  They  caught  Turtle,  Cricket  went
into  a  hole,  and  Mosquito  lighted  on  a  place  in  the  fire.  They  were  going
to  put  Turtle  into  the  fire,  but  he  said  that  he  was  not  afraid  of  the  fire
and  that  he  wished  they  would  put  him  in,  for  he  would  scatter  the  fire  all
over  the  room.  At  last  the  people  said:  "Let  us  throw  him  into  the
water."  Turtle  cried  and  said:  "I  am  afraid  of  the  water."  The  people
said:  "  He  is  afraid  of  the  water;  let  us  throw  him  into  the  water."  They
threw  him  into  the  water,  and  when  he  struck  the  water  he  raised  his  head,
poked  his  tongue  out  to  the  people,  and  said:  "The  water  is  my  home;  I

'Told  by  Thief,  Kitkehahki.  This  story  is  told  to  the  children  to  teach  them
that  they  should  not  join  a  war  party  which  had  weak  men  in  it,  but  that  they
should  join  a  strong  party,  and  theirs  would  be  successful.

fooled  you."  The  other  members  of  the  war  party  were  not  found.  The
people  knew  that  they  were  still  in  the  lodge,  but  they  could  not  find  them.
Finally,  Mosquito  went  out  of  the  lodge  and  flew  into  a  swampy  country,
where  he  got  his  legs  stuck  in  the  mud.  Ever  since  the  time  of  the  Tur-
tle's war  party,  crickets  have  lived  in  people's  lodges,  and  mosquitoes  have
lived  near  swampy  places.

148.  THE  ANIMALS'  WAR  PARTY.'

Many  of  the  people  once  gathered  together  and  went  on  the  war-path.
They  had  heard  of  three  men  who  lived  at  a  certain  place  who  were  very
hard  to  kill.  Many  people  had  tried  to  kill  them,  but  none  had  ever  been
successful,  and  the  ground  about  their  camp  was  covered  with  skulls  of
those  who  had  tried  and  failed.  Among  the  many  people  who  went  out
on  the  war-path  were  three  little  warriors.  Rabbit,  Turtle,  and  Spider-
Woman.  When  they  were  near  the  lodge  of  the  three  men  who  were  hard
to  kill,  the  three  little  warriors  boasted  that  they  were  going  to  kill  them.
They  told  all  the  men  to  get  their  bows  and  arrows  ready;  that  they  were
about  to  make  an  attack.  Rabbit  charged,  riding  a  mule,  and  singing
this  song:

I  make  the  charge  on  the  first  man,

Look  out!     Look  out!

Thus  they  are  frightened  away.

Then  Turtle  came  with  a  spear  and  something  on  his  back,  and  he  also
sang  a  song.  The  spear  that  Turtle  had  was  of  grass,  and  the  thing  that

  "passage_text": "A  man  in  dream  sees  monster  of  immense  size  with  head  of  many  colors  sur-\nmounted by  white  eagle  feather.  He  decides  to  visit  place  where  he  had  vision\nof  monster.  On  river  bank  he  sees  water  spouting.  Monster  lifts  its  head  up\nand  down  from  water  four  times,  drawing  its  breath  and  drawing  man  toward\nwater.  On  opening  his  eyes  he  finds  monster  and  animals  of  all  kinds.  Monster\nproclaims  that  it  controls  all  water  beings.  He  is  taught  mysteries  of  animals\nand  their  ways  of  doctoring.  Man  on  his  way  home  collects  willows  with  which\nto  make  image  of  monster  in  his  lodge,  and  kills  some  buffalo,  one  of  which  he  is  to\nuse  in  making  effigy.  Lacking  further  information  as  to  how  to  construct  effigy,\nhe  is  visited  in  vision  by  monster  and  is  told  how  to  capture  eagle  in  order  to  obtain\nfeather  for  head.  He  is  told  to  go  to  eagle's  nest.  The  eagles  are  unable  to  help\nhim  and  he  meets  wild-cat,  representing  sky  and  stars,  which  teaches  him  how  to\ncheat  people.  Evening-Star  then  addresses  him  and  gives  him  com.  Next,  wood-\npecker helps  him  with  stick  upon  which  to  tie  corn,  explaining  that  when  bundle  is\ncomplete  it  shall  be  efficacious  in  bringing  rain.  Ducks  offer  to  assist,  and  next\nOwls,  and  next  the  four  gods  in  heavens.  Different  animals  also  visit  him  in  his\nvisions  and  give  him  songs.  He  also  receives  a  song  from  Sun  as  it  comes  up.  He\nis  also  taught  how  he  may  decorate  child  to  represent  Tirawa  during  ceremony,  red\nline  of  paint  around  face  indicating  that  Sun  has  touched  child.  Child  is  to  be\nplaced  on  nest  of  oriole,  thus  showing  that  its  path  should  be  hard  but  safe,  for\noriole's  nest  is  high  in  tree  and  can  not  be  blown  away  by  storms  nor  can  snakes\nget  at  it.  He  is  further  instructed  that  child  is  to  be  permitted  to  return  home\nand  that  paint  on  its  face  is  to  be  allowed  to  wear  off.\n\n13.  THE   GIRL   WHO   MARRIED   A   STAR.\n\nOne  of  two  girls  sleeping  in  summer  arbor  wishes  that  she  might  marry  star.\nAwakening,  she  finds  herself  in  strange  country,  wife  of  star.  She  is  warned  not  to\ndig  turnips,  but  does  so  after  birth  of  boy.  While  digging  she  sees  earth  below  and\npeople  walking  around.  She  saves  sinew  of  animals  killed  by  her  husband  and\nmakes  rope  by  which  she  descends  with  boy,  but  rope  does  not  quite  reach  earth.\nHer  husband  discovers  her  absence,  drops  stone  downward,  which  kills  her.  Boy\nremains  near  his  mother  for  several  days.  During  thunder  shower  boy  follows  dry\npath  until  he  comes  to  tipi  occupied  by  old  woman  and  her  grandson.  The  two\nboys  grow  up  together.  They  are  warned  not  to  go  to  certain  dangerous  places,\ndisobey,  and  destroy  certain  monsters — bears,  monster,  mountain-lion,  and  other\nwicked  animals.  Afterwards  boys  return  to  their  country,  where  Star-Boy  becomes\ngreat  man.     He  disappears  and  is  supposed  to  have  returned  to  heaven."
}

  "passage_text": "ABSTRACTS.  479\n\n14.  THE  GRAIN-OF-CORN  BUNDLE.\n\nMan  of  prairie  hears  woman  crying,  and  going  to  place  finds  no  one  there.  He\ndreams  that  night  of  seeing  woman,  who  speaks  to  him.  The  next  night  he  goes\nwhere  he  had  been  told  to  meet  woman,  who  is  beautiful.  She  is  grain  of  corn,\nhaving  her  origin  in  Evening-Star.  She  tells  man  to  carry  her  with  him,  keeping\nher  in  his  quiver.  Man  goes  on  war-path  and  his  guardian  informs  him  of  enemy.\nAccording  to  instructions,  he  makes  sacred  bundle,  which  contains  com.  While  off\nto  gambling  ground  one  day  his  mother  opens  bundle  and  converses  with  corn.\nOn  his  return,  com  tells  him  of  fact.  She  also  helps  him  on  war-path,  but  asks  him\nto  refrain  from  marrying  for  two  years  and  to  plant  her  as  seed  corn.  At  proper\ntime  man  marries  and  his  descendants  are  many.  He  leaves  instructions  obtained\nfrom  Com- Woman  concerning  ceremonies,  especially  those  respecting  planting  of\ncom.\n\n15.  THE   METEORITE   PEOPLE.\n\nWonderful  being,  Pahokatawa,  is  killed  and  cut  up  by  enemy,  and  animals\ndevour  his  flesh,  but  heavenly  gods  agree  to  restore  him  and  signify  their  desire\nto  earthly  gods,  who  go  and  restore  meat  and  bones,  but  can  not  find  man's  brains.\nAfterwards,  he  visits  earth  from  time  to  time  as  meteorite,  often  warning  them  of\nenemy,  and  telling  people  that  they  must  not  be  afraid  of  meteors  or  shooting  stars.\nAfterwards,  men  walking  over  prairie  dig  out  bright-colored  stone  in  shape  of\nturnip.  They  regard  it  as  meteor  sent  by  Pahokatawa.  Offerings  are  made  to  it,\nand  it  is  believed  to  be  part  of  Morning-Star.  It  is  believed  that  as  long  as\nstone  is  present,  diseases  could  not  enter  camp.\n\n16.   BUFFALO  WIFE  AND  CORN  WIFE.\n\nYoung  man  in  village  does  not  associate  with  other  boys,  but  daily  climbs  hill,\nwhere  he  remains  by  himself,  paying  special  care  to  his  personal  adornment.  On\nhis  return  in  evening,  he  is  an  eagle.  Once  while  on  hill  he  hears  singing  coming\nfrom  Buffalo  women  in  east  and  calling  some  one  in  west.  Each  woman  has  pair\nof  moccasins,  and  while, he  is  thinking  which  one  to  accept,  one  places  one  on  one\nfoot  and  other  one  on  other  foot,  and  he  decides  to  marry  them  both.  With  his\nwives  he  retums  and,  with  his  mother,  they  all  live  together.  Buffalo- Wife  gives\nbirth  to  boy  and  Com-Wife  to  girl.  The  children  quarrel  over  spoon  and  ear  of  com.\nMothers  become  angry  and  Buffalo- Wife  leaves  with  her  child.  Corn-Wife  and  her\nchild  disappear  under  ground.  Man  assumes  shape  of  eagle  and  flies  toward  east\nuntil  he  comes  to  his  Buffalo-Wife  and  son,  now  a  calf.  At  night  she  turns  into\n,  woman  and  selects  her  tipi.  Eagle-Man  becomes  man,  enters  the  tipi,  but  is  re-\npulsed by  his  wife,  though  his  little  boy  plays  with  him.  In  morning,  wife  and  child\nturn  into  buffalo,  and  leave.  He  follows  them  as  before,  on  across  stream  of  water.\nThey  cross  high  mountains  and  finally  enter  woman's  village,  where  man  is\nasked  to  pick  out  his  wife  from  other  cows  and  his  son  from  other  calves.  Before\nentering  her  lodge  he  calms  fierce  bear,  whereby  rock  entrance  to  her  lodge  opens.\nPassing  through,  entrance  falls,  but  he  is  unhurt,  as  he  turns  into  breath  feather.\nHe  is  able  to  distinguish  his  wife,  being  instructed  by  his  son  to  look  for  mark  he  has\n\n480  THE  pawnee:  mythology.\n\nplaced  on  her  tail.  Husband  is  invited  into  sweat-lodge,  where  he  finds  bulls  which\nattempt  to  prevent  him  from  going  out.  When  steam  heat  becomes  oppressive  he\nturns  into  badger  and  thus  is  able  to  get  his  nose  from  under  lodge  and  so  can  stand\nheat.  Then  husband  is  sent  to  tree  with  eagle  nest  in  it,  where  storm  rages,  with\nlightning.  On  his  addressing  eagles  storm  ceases.  He  returns  with  wood.  He  is\nchallenged  to  run  race  with  old  buffalo  cow,  race  to  be  to  the  four  ends  of  earth.\nShould  he  win,  people  are  to  live  upon  buffalo;  otherwise,  buffalo  are  to  feed  upon\nhuman  beings.  He  turns  himself  into  Magpie  and  they  start.  The  old  woman  cow,\npointing  with  her  cane  in  direction,  is  at  once  there.  Thus  she  gains  on  Eagle-Man,\nbut  at  his  request  Badgers  dig  holes  into  which  she  falls.  Thus  he  begins  to  gain.\nHe  wins,  and  buffalo  are  released  from  cave.  Certain  spotted  buffalo  are  driven\nback,  together  with  buffalo  with  two  heads.  White  buffalo,  however,  escapes.  Then\nold  woman  tries  to  make  love  to  Eagle-Man  and  warns  him  not  to  drink  water  from\nragged  woman.  He  does  so,  thus  e.xciting  people,  who  accuse  him  of  drinking\nchief's  water,  as  ragged  woman  was  chief's  wife.  Chief  becomes  angry  and  digs  up\nearth.  Although  his  body  is  nothing  but  bones,  he  is  chief  of  buffalo.  Eagle-\nMan  attempts  to  shoot  him,  and  is  told  by  Mocking-Bird  that  vulnerable  part  of\nchief  is  hole  in  his  chest.  Thus  Eagle-Man  kills  buffalo  chief.  Thereafter  buffalo\nscatter  and  Eagle-Man  returns  to  his  people.\n\n17.   THE    POOR   BOY   WHO    MARRIED   THE    CHIEF'S    DAUGHTER."

  "passage_text": "BUFFALO.\n\nWitch-Woman  lives  in  prairie  by  herself  with  her  Poor  Boy  and  four  powerful\ndogs.  Boy  has  black  bow  with  two  strings  and  four  black  arrows.  He  is  great\nhunter.  From  time  to  time  he  is  urged  by  witch  to  kill  human  beings  for  her\nfood.  Boy  always  escapes  capture  because  of  magic  flight  of  his  arrow.  Buffalo\nknowing  woman's  habits,  become  angry,  hold  council,  and  send  two  young  buffalo  to\nget  boy  to  kill  him,  thus  stopping  witch's  supply  of  meat.    Boy  in  meantime,  sitting\n\nABSTRACTS.  48l\n\non  hill,  has  vision,  goes  to  his  grandmother  and  tells  her  that  he  is  about  to  make\njourney.     She  asks  for  four  additional  bodies,  which  he  succeeds  in  securing.     As  he\nis  leaving  he  instructs  witch  as  to  care  of  dogs,  one  of  them  to  be  kept  tied  all  the\ntime.    He  travels  many  days  without  food  and  encounters  two  buffalo,  one  of  which\nhe  shoots.    As  he  is  about  to  eat  one  of  kidneys,  Buffalo  speaks  to  him,  directing  him\nto  put  back  piece  of  meat  he  has  in  his  hand  and  to  look  away.     Turning  back,  he\nsees  woman  wearing  new  buffalo  robe.     She  restores  life  to  fallen  Buffalo.    They  fol-\nlow boy  to  hollow,  where  they  turn  into  women  to  secure  from  him  details  of  secret\nof  his  ability  to  kill  human  beings  and  elude  pursuit.    Women  start  to  return  to  their\ncountry  as  Buffalo,  and  boy  follows.     At  night  Buffalo  become  women  again  and\nobtain  further  details  of  his  secret.     He  even  relates  how  he  may  be  killed.     They\napproach  Buffalo  village,  where  he  sees  Buffalo  playing  with  game  sticks.     He  is\nwarned  by  old  Buffalo  that  Buffalo  wish  to  kill  him.     Old  Buffalo  is  chief,  who  lives\nin  west  and  promises  to  help  boy.  Boy  follows  him,  and  he  instructs  him  that  he  is  to\ndive  four  times  in  pond  in  front  of  tipi  of  Buffalo  who  has  white  spot  on  his  fore-\nhead and  who  is  especially  desirous  of  killing  boy.     He  does  so,  and  White  Spot\nrefuses  to  take  his  usual  bath.     Boy  is  challenged  to  smoke  contest  with  White\nSpot,  but  is  directed  by  Buffalo  chief  as  to  secret  of  victory.     In  contest  they  are  to\nsee  who  can  cause  smoke  to  ascend  the  higher.     Boy  wins,  as  smoke  from  his  pipe\nascends  on  one  side  of  the  tree  and  comes  down  on  other.     Next,  drinking  contest  is\nproposed,  the  object  being  to  drain  pond.     Again  boy  is  assisted,  and  during  contest\nuses  horns  given  him  by  Buffalo  chief,  which  enable  him  to  be  victorious.     On  fol-\nlowing day  runners  are  to  race,  but  the  Buffalo  on  boy's  side  win,  as  he  lashes  them\nwith  his  bow  string.     Boy  now  strings  his  bow  and  kills  several  Buffalo,  but  White\nSpot's  friends  attack  him  and  he  disappears.     Then  White  Spot  appeals  to  Buffalo\nwomen  as  to  how  to  take  boy,  who  tell  him  that  he  keeps  ahead  by  magic  of  his  bow,\nwhich  is  black  snake.     They  finally  draw  near  him  and  he  hides  in  bunch  of  grass,\nfrom  which  he  is  blown  by  bull.     Boy  disappears  and  hides  in  pond,  which  Buffalo\ndrink  dry.     As  Buffalo  blows  his  breath  on  mud  hole  in  center,  boy  jumps  on  dry\nland  and  then  disappears.     He  goes  to  timber  and  climbs  high  tree.     Boy  urinates\nin  his  robe,  drops  of  which  fall  upon  bulls,  who  think  it  is  rain  because  boy  has  been\nkilled,  for  they  see  no  clouds.    Presently  bulls  discover  boy  and  they  select  five  bulls\nto  butt  down  tree,  first  trying  to  lift  it  up  by  the  roots.     As  tree  begins  to  totter,\nboy  yells. They  return  home  and  boy  tells  his  grand-\nmother to  go  north  with  bag  of  seeds,  and  to  plant  seeds,  and  to  depend  on  them  for\nher  food.     He  releases  his  dog  and  puts  on  his  costume. Clam  Shell  would  carry  out  some  like  babies,\nand  some  would  be  in  shape  of  birds.  Some  of  signs  have  come  to  pass.  Moon  has\nturned  black  several  times,  but  time  for  end  of  world  is  not  yet  come.  Time  will  be\ndetermined  by  North  and  South  Stars. He  is  so  ashamed  that  he\nleaves  and  is  never  heard  of.\n\n37.    THE    HERMAPHRODITE.\n\nYoung  man,  caring  nothing  for  women,  is  visited  by  young  girl.  He  bathes  in\nspring. He  is  so  ashamed  he  commits  suicide  rather  than  be  hermaphrodite.\n\n38. Scouts  report  small  village,  which  they  attack  and  find\nmany  enemies.  They  are  surrounded  and  all  scalped.  After  enemy  leave  they\ncome  together,  and  leader  as  spokesman  declares  that  being  scalped  they  would  be\nashamed  to  return  to  their  people.  They  agree  to  live  among  hills. HANDSOME-BOY  AND  AFTER-BIRTH  BOY.\n\nPoor  boy  likes  chief's  daughter  and  is  invited  by  her  to  her  lodge.  Boy  does\nnot  go,  fearing  chief. They  ascend  with  him  in  rising  smoke.\n\n40.     LONG-TOOTH-BOY.\n\nA  man  and  his  wife  travel  east  to  country  of  small  ponds  where  they  live  by\nthemselves  for  many  years.  Woman  gives  birth  to  child  and  dies,  after-birth  being\nthrown  by  father  into  water.  He  feeds  child  with  animals'  milk.  In  his  absence\nstrange  boy  comes  and  plays  with  his  son.  He  has  long  teeth  and  is  called  Long-\nTooth-Boy.  Older  son  tells  his  father  of  strange  boy  and  he  plans  to  capture  him  by\nstrategy,  first  turning  into  parfleche;  but  Long-Tooth-Boy  recognizes  him  and  jumps\ninto  pond.  Man  mourns  and  is  addressed  by  buffalo,  who  tells  him  to  kill  him,  remove\nhis  bladder,  fill  it  with  air,  and  tie  it  to  head  of  Long-Tooth-Boy.  This  is  done,  and  so\nLong-Tooth-Boy  is  captured  in  water.  Boys  are  warned  against  visiting  dangerous\nplaces.  They  disobey,  visit  steep  bank,  where  they  encounter  water  monster,  which\nhas  swallowed  their  father.  Leaving  their  bows  and  arrows  on  bank  they  fill  their\npockets  with  stones,  slide  down  beaver  path,  and  as  they  touch  water  they  turn  into\nfoam.  Foam  floats  down  river  and  into  mouth  of  monster.  Then  they  become\nhuman  beings,  but  do  not  find  their  father.  They  make  their  way  out  and  Long-\nTooth-Boy  breaks  his  bow  and  arrows  and  plays  with  them  inside  monster's\nmouth.  With  flint  stones  he  makes  spark  which  he  throws  inside  monster,  and  bow\nand  arrows  are  burned.  Suddenly  monster  bursts  and  is  thrown  upon  ground.\nWith  sinew  strings  they  drag  home  its  skin,  which  they  had  blown  off.  They  give\nit  to  their  father  for  tobacco  pouch.  They  go  to  river,  attempt  to  cross  on  fallen\nlog,  but  old  woman  on  opposite  side  causes  log  to  stand  on  end  and  grow  up  like  tree.\nShe  spits  upon  it;  it  grows  cold  and  sleets.  Around  tree  are  many  human  skulls.\nOld  woman  leaves,  thinking  they  will  soon  perish.  Long-Tongue-Boy  gnaws  steps\non  tree  whereby  they  descend.  They  plan  the  old  woman's  death.  Long-Tooth-\nBoy  becomes  raccoon,  which  older  brother  kills,  and  at  old  woman's  request  takes\nit  into  her  lodge.  Inside  lodge  he  places  meat  in  pot,  and  on  top,  head  resting\nupon  paws,  being  careful  not  to  cut  intestines.  Big  fire  is  kindled  under  pot  and\nsoon  raccoon  sticks  out  its  tongue,  which  is  signal  for  older  brother  to  leave  lodge.\nOld  woman,  owing  to  heat  in  lodge,  has  removed  her  garments;  pot  now  boils  over\nand  splashes  on  woman,  who  falls  toward  fire  and  is  killed. THE  DOG-BOY  WHO  MARRIED  THE   CHIEF'S  DAUGHTER.\n\nWhite  Moccasin's  wife  gives  birth  to  dog,  which  he  throws  into  creek. Looking  around,  he  finds  that  he  is  now  boy.\nLooking  around  again  he  discovers  quiver.  He  goes  to  his  village,  where  he  announces\nthat  he  is  White  Moccasin's  child;  is  taken  to  chief's  lodge,  where  he  remains.  On\nbuffalo  hunt  he  is  leading  spirit,  and  returning  marries  chief's  daughter.  They  have\nmany  children.  One  day  he  goes  south,  sees  deer,  looks  again  and  deer  has  become\ngirl,  who  warns  that  his  father  is  trying  to  kill  him,  but  that  she  will  protect\nhim.  Boy  returns,  invites  men  to  his  lodge,  including  his  father,  and  challenges  him\nto  contest.  His  father  has  no  power  over  him,  but  boy  waves  his  hand  and  his\nfather  begins  to  butt  his  head  against  everything  he  encounters.  White  Mocca-\nsin's friends  try  to  kill  boy  with  clubs,  and  he  yells,  and  his  enemies,  including  his\nfather,  fall  down."

He  is  good  hunter,  bringing  home  much  game,\nbut  treats  his  wife  meanly  and  she  tries  to  leave  him,  though  is  always  unsuccessful,\nfinding  herself  at  each  attempt  inside  rattle  hanging  at  his  belt. He  becomes\nman  and  people  abuse  him,  saying  that  he  belongs  in  heavens  and  has  no  right  to\nmistreat  an  earthly  woman.  He  throws  rattle  on  ground  and  woman  wakes  up.\nHe  pulls  string  of  his  rattle,  she  enters,  and  he  takes  her  home  and  releases  her.  He\nnow  repents  and  returns,  placing  her  in  his  rattle  and  takes  her  home.  He  becomes\nSun- Ray  and  goes  back  to  sun.\n\n55.    HAWK    SLAYS   THE    FIRE-KEEPER.\n\nIn  beginning.  Fire- Keeper  has  his  home  with  people  in  west,  but  he  does  not  like\nthem.  On  west  of  their  village  is  deep  river,  across  which  live  two  Hawk  brothers.\nThey  have  magic  log  by  which  they  cross  river.  Older  crosses  and  gets  wife,  daugh-\nter of  priest.  Fire- Keeper,  priest's  brother,  decides  to  kill  young  man,  because  he\nwas  not  consulted  regarding  marriage. Being  strips  him  of  his  clothing  and  bums  it  and  he  loses  his\neyes.  His  captor  leads  him  for  many  days  till  they  arrive  at  his  home,  where  he  is\nmade  slave. At  his  request  she  leads  him  on  rocky  hill  with  steep  sides,\nplaces  him  at  edge  with  his  feet  hanging  down,  and  pushes  him  over  at  his  earnest  re-\nquest before  sunrise.  She  starts  toward  foot  of  precipice  and  encounters  her  husband\nin  his  normal  condition,  fully  costumed.  He  starts  forward  to  revenge  himself  on  her\nuncle,  and  she  goes  to  her  brother-in-law  and  they  go  to  her  people,  who  are  await-\ning her  husband.  At  night  they  see  fire  flying  through  sky  and  they  know  that  he\nhas  killed  Fire- Keeper.  He  did  this  by  turning  into  Hawk,  striking  Fire-Keeper\non  head.  Then  turning  into  human  being,  he  threw  fire  through  sky  in  different\ndirections,  announcing  that  warriors  should  receive  help  from  stars'  light. which  he  takes  home.  From  this  time  on  he  brings  larger  buffalo  home  each  day.
Grandmother  jerks  meat  and  stores  it  in  parfleches.  Girl  visits  lodge  and  is  fed.
Boy  again  encounters  his  benefactor,  who  gives  him  full  costume.  He  asks  his
grandmother  to  go  to  chief's  lodge  and  ask  for  his  girl  in  marriage.  Chief  promises
his  answer  next  day.  In  meantime  youngest  daughter  of  chief  again  visits  them
and  tells  of  her  love  for  boy.  She  carries  meat  home,  which  she  gives  to  her  parents
in  night.  On  old  woman's  return  next  day  chief  consents  to  his  daughter's  mar-
riage. He  enters  chief's  tipi,  and  being  finely  arrayed  other  daughters,  who  formerly
despised  him,  now  wish  to  marry  him.  He  takes  youngest  daughter  back  to  his
grandmother's  lodge,  where  they  have  feast,  inviting  chief.  People  are  starving
and  boy  calls  buffalo  four  times,  and  buffalo  become  numerous.  Boy  remains  faith-
ful to  his  young  wife.     They  have  many  children.

60.    THE    BUFFALO   AND   RED-SPIDER-WOMAN'S    DAUGHTER.

Red-Spider-Woman,  living  in  center  of  earth,  controls  com,  beans,  etc.,  and  has
many  daughters.  Buffalo  live  in  north,  their  chief  having  son  named  Curly-Eyes.
Buffalo  in  council  decide  to  send  four  of  their  number  to  south  to  look  for  better
land,  Curly-Eyes  being  one  of  party.  On  their  journey  they  meet  Red-Spider-
Woman  and  her  daughters,  Curly-Eyes  falling  in  love  with  one  of  them.  Reporting
fact  to  his  father,  he  is  told  it  will  be  necessary  to  buy  her  in  order  that  he  may  bring
her  home.  Then  delegations  are  sent  offering  old  woman,  first,  valley  full  of  buffalo,
then  two  valleys  full,  then  half  land  full,  and  finally  land  full.  Still  old  woman
refuses,  whereupon  buffalo  decide  to  move  to  her  country.  They  travel  south  many
years.  Curly-Eyes  and  other  buffalo  see  girl.  Old  woman's  fields  are  trampled.
She  stands  on  prairie  and  begins  to  disappear  in  ground.  They  kill  her.  Buffalo
chief  announces  that  her  body  shall  remain  in  ground  as  medicinal  root,  from  which
is  derived  squash  medicine.     Hereafter  buffalo  cover  earth.

61.  THE    SINGING    BUFFALO    CALF.

Buffalo  calf  traveling  with  party  dreams  that  they  are  to  be  surrounded,
killed,  and  consecrated.  Dream  comes  true.  Buffalo  are  satisfied  as  long  as  they
are  consecrated.

62.  THE  BUFFALO  AND  THE  DEER.

Buffalo  and  deer  dispute  concerning  relative  merits  of  their  meat  for  the
purpose  of  consecration.  Deer  becomes  angry,  and,  running  amongst  the  people
who  are  on  hunt,  is  shot  and  consecrated.  Consequently,  deer  are  always  first  con-
secrated when  upon  hunt.

63.  THE  UNFAITHFUL  BUNDLE-KEEPER.

Famine  prevails.  Buffalo  are  far  in  west.  They  have  council  and  decide  that
chief's  daughter  should  lead  them  to  people.  She  puts  bundle  on  her  back  and
divides  them  into  four  herds,  first  herd  being  sent  to  south  of  village  and  is  killed.
Second  herd  fares  same  on  north  side,  and  still  third.  Fourth  herd  approaches
village  from  west,  she  remaining  behind  with  bundle.     During  slaughter  of  this  herd

she  gives  birth  to  calf  in  ravine  and  joins  those  who  escape  slaughter,  who  now  return
home.  Calf  is  taught  by  Wind  name  of  its  father  and  mother,  and  starts  home  sing-
ing of  its  parentage.  People  are  surprised,  for  they  thought  girl  maiden.  When
chief  is  assured  that  girl  is  mother  of  calf,  she  is  commanded  to  cease  carrying  sacred
bundle.  Henceforth,  witch  woman  shall  not  carry  bundle,  and  women  of  high  birth,
though  unmarried,  occasionally  have  children.

64.    THE  HUNGRY  COYOTE.

Coyote  is  famishing,  hears  tramp  of  buffalo  and  sees  calf.  He  questions  calf,
who  sings  to  him,  in  meantime  passing  on  by  and  thus  escaping  with  its  life,  while
Coyote  dies  of  hunger.

65.    THE  GATHERING  OF  THE  PRIESTS.

In  village  of  Coyotes  they  are  about  to  open  sacred  bundle  and  women  are  told
to  bring  firewood,  but  they  are  on  hunt,  except  one  girl.  She  grinds  com  and
makes  mush,  which  she  takes  to  priests'  lodge.  Priests  are  very  grateful  and  sing
her  praises.  Buffalo  hunters  are  unsuccessful,  but,  because  of  mush,  priests  keep
bundle  open,  singing  all  night.     In  morning  hunters  are  successful.

66.  THE  MAN  WHO  SANG  TO  COYOTE.

In  winter  time  people  tell  Coyote  stories.  It  is  winter  time,  and  in  every  lodge
they  are  telling  Coyote  tales.  Young  man  goes  on  hunt,  encounters  Coyote,  and
starts  to  shoot  him,  but  stops  for  fear  of  bad  luck.  Thereafter  he  is  lucky  while  on
hunt,  for  sparing  Coyote's  life.

67.    HOW  THE   CANNIBAL   SPIDER-WOMAN   WAS    OVERCOME."

They  are  warned  by\ndaughter  against  old  woman,  especially  not  to  eat  of  food  which  she  will  ofifer  them,\nfor  it  will  be  human  flesh.  They  are  welcomed  to  old  woman's  lodge,  are  offered\nfood,  of  which  they  eat,  first  having  eaten  some  medicine.  Boys  leave  lodge  and\nemetic  takes  effect.  Again  they  take  medicine  and  eat  of  bowl  of  human  eyes,  and\nagain  they  go  out  and  allow  emetic  to  take  effect.  Following  morning  they  are  fed\nsquash,  which  is  human  ears.  They  vomit  it  up.  They  prepare  to  play  game,\ncovering  their  bodies  with  white  clay,  and  from  their  eyes  extend  little  black  streaks.\nThey  begin  to  dance  up  and  down  by  steep  bank,  which  old  woman  pushes  her  vic-\ntims over.  As  they  dance  old  woman  sings  of  snowstorm  and  other  storms,  but  boys\nturn  into  snowbirds.  She  sings  of  air  and  they  become  larks.  She  then  acknowl-\nedges defeat  and  offers  her  daughter  to  boys.  They  express  wish  to  continue  game;\nand  they  sing  about  storms,  etc.  Old  woman  survives  until  they  sing  of  grasshoppers,\nwhich  fly  around  and  under  her  and  take  her  up  to  Moon,  hanging  from  which\noften  a  piece  of  her  dress  may  be  seen.  Grasshoppers  continue  their  flight  to  Sun,\nwhere  they  may  be  seen  in  summer  time.\n\n74.   THE   GIRL,   SPIDER-WOMAN,   AND  THE   BALL  GAME.\n\nLame  man  and  his  niece  live  alone.  He  disappears  each  day,  often  remaining\naway  late,  which  angers  girl,  and  she  tells  him  not  to  go  so  far  away.  Once  while  he\nis  gone  being  takes  girl  to  far  country  in  wind.  There  she  meets  Spider- Woman,\nwho  tells  her  that  she  must  play  game  of  double  ball.  Girl  cries  and  is  taken  to\nlodge  of  Wood-Rat.  Errand  man  appears  that  evening  and  invites  girl  to  feast  with\nSpider-Woman.  Girl  goes  to  Spider-Woman's  lodge,  who  whispers  to  herself  that\nshe  will  place  girl's  head  among  her  skulls.  Girl  refuses  to  eat  human  eyes,  and  in\nnight  she  asks  birds  to  tell  her  uncle  that  she  needs  his  help.  Girl  asks  for  four  days'\ntime  and  goes  to  hill  and  cries.  In  meantime  uncle  returns,  misses  girl,  takes  double\nball  game  from  bundle,  places  himself  on  them,  strikes  his  ankle  with  stick,  making\nmotion  as  if  throwing  balls  into  air,  and  balls  carry  him.  Thus  he  goes  south  look-\ning for  his  niece,  then  west,  then  north.  Not  finding  her,  he  returns  home  and  a\nlittle  bird  offers  to  lead  him  to  his  niece,  and  flies  toward  east.  Uncle  finds  niece\nand  he  gives  her  double  ball  with  which  to  play,  and  blows  his  breath  on  string  so\nthat  it  will  not  break.  When  time  for  game  comes,  uncle  tells  her  to  strike  him\nseveral  times  upon  his  ankle  with  stick.  Game  begins.  As  they  progress,  string\nholding  balls  breaks,  and  Spider-Woman  suggests  that  they  stop,  but  girl  insists\nthat  they  should  use  her  set.  She  begins  to  beat  her  uncle's  feet  and  presently\ntwin  balls  appear.  Thereafter  she  is  uniformly  successful,  finally  winning  Spider-\nWoman  and  her  people.  Old  Woman  is  killed  and  burned,  and  jumps  from  fire  into\ngrass  as  spider.  Girl  whips  her  uncle's  feet,  placing  balls  near  them,  and  thus  they\nenter  his  feet  again,  and  he  says  that  so  it  is  that  they  rid  themselves  of  Spider-\nWoman,  and  that  hereafter  people  may  have  rheumatism  and  require  bent  sticks  for\nsupport.\n\n5o8  THE  pawnee:  mythology.\n\n75.   THE   BOY   WHO   KILLED   THE   CANNIBAL  WITCH.\n\nYoung  man  wandered  about  country,  finding  many  human  skulls.  He  finds\nlodge  about  which  are  playing  three  ugly  girls  and  one  beautiful  girl.  Three  ugly\ngirls  enter  lodge  and  youngest  warns  him  against  her  mother,  who  is  cannibal.  In\nmorning  young  man  is  asked  into  lodge,  is  offered  food  repeatedly,  but  it  has  no  effect\nupon  him.  Old  woman  challenges  him  to  dance,  but  he  becomes  snowbird  and\nthen  lark,  whereupon  he  carries  old  woman  up  to  moon.  Then  he  returns,  dismisses\nthree  oldest  girls  and  takes  youngest  girl  to  his  village  as  his  wife.  She  prepares\ngarden  and  plants  different  kinds  of  seeds.  In  meantime  he  goes  to  west  and  brings\nbuffalo,  which  power  he  has  obtained  from  larks.\n\n76.    THE    WITCH-WOMAN   AND    HER   HOME.\n\nHunter  goes  east  to  grass-lodge,  which  he  is  invited  to  enter  by  Witch- Woman.\nHe  partakes  of  food,  dies,  and  his  head  is  hung  up  in  her  lodge.  After  four  days  his\nwife  sends  her  son  to  look  for  his  father.  She  challenges  boy  to  dance,  but  first  she\nsuspends  about  his  neck  his  father's  head,  which  is  held  in  place  by  cord  pass-\ning from  ear  to  ear.  Witch- Woman  is  about  to  kill  boy,  rescuers  appear,  and  she  is\nburned.     She  bursts  open  and  croaking  tree  frog  springs  upon  tree.\n\n77.    THE    MEDICINE-CHILD    AND   THE    BEAVER    MEDICINE."
}

He  returns,  obtains  his\nbelongings,  while  she  obtains  hers,  and  they  journey  south,  killing  game  as  they  go.\nHer  relatives  ask  chief's  son  her  whereabouts.  Careful  examination  of  young  men\nin  village  reveals  absence  of  poor  boy,  and  it  is  known  he  has  left  with  chief's  daugh-\nter. Poor  boy  and  girl  travel  south  to  Pahuk,  where  they  make  grass-lodge  and  live.\nAs  she  is  getting  water  in  pond  she  sees  Loon,  and  later  finds  nest  with  two  young\nbirds. Loons  tell  them  that  they  will  have  no\nchildren;  but  that  they  will  give  them  their  power. At  Loons'  suggestion  man  goes\non  hunt  and  returns  with  many  ponies.  Loons  are  anxious  that  they  should  all\nreturn  to  their  village,  and  they  start  out,  woman  carrying  Loons.  They  enter\nvillage  and  people  are  frightened,  thinking  they  are  enemy,  for  they  had  been  gone\nfour  years.  Man  gives  several  ponies  to  chief's  son  and  tells  him  he  has  been  to\nPahuk,  and  chief's  son  invites  him  and  Loons  to  eat  with  them.  War  party  is\nformed  and  ponies  are  brought  home.  Chief's  son  then  leads  war  party  and  poor\nboy  assists  him,  and  they  take  one  of  Loons  with  them,  which  guides  and  protects\nthem.  They  return  with  scalps  and  ponies.  They  again  go  on  war  party  and  young\nman  of  village  attempts  to  visit  young's  man  wife,  but  Loon  which  has  remained\nwith  her  makes  noise  in  protest  and  is  mistreated.  On  that  night  woman's  husband\non  war-path  knows  that  something  is  wrong  and  they  set  out  for  home.  Arriving,  he\nfinds  Loon  is  ill,  and  it  tells  man  that  his  wife  has  been  unfaithful  during  his  absence,\nand  that  man  who  has  been  with  her  has  mistreated  him.  Loon  dies.  Young  man\ntakes  his  skin,  and  shortly  after  skin  of  other  Loon,  which  also  dies.  Then  he  drives\nhis  wife  from  his  lodge,  telling  her  never  to  return.  Thereafter,  Loons  are  used  on\naltar  of  medicine-man.  He  finally  dies  of  broken  heart,  but  leaves  his  medicines  to\nchief's  son."

She  tells\nher  father  to  make  his  bed  on  north  side  of  stone,  which  he  shall  keep  in  lodge,  and\nthat  stone  will  speak  to  him. Farther  in  he  will  find  himself  in  large\nlodge,  where  he  will  hear  animals  playing  on  notched  stick;  that  animals  will  go\nto  entrance,  see  stone,  and  ask  man  to  remove  it;  that  he  is  to  tell  animals  that  he\nwill  remove  stone  if  they  will  give  him  their  power. Root  is  then  carried  to  man's  tipi,  which  has  been  swept  and\nnew  mats  placed  on  ground. He  becomes  a  great  medicine-man.\n\n83.    ORIGIN   OF  THE   GEESE   MEDICINE.\n\nYoung  man  who  often  goes  with  war  parties  is  in  love  and  often  visits  spring  to\nsee  girl,  but  she  flees  from  him.  He  therefore  tries  to  associate  with  other  girls  in\norder  to  provoke  her  jealousy,  and  thinks  that  thus  he  may  win  her,  but  all  girls\nrefuse  to  associate  with  him,  and  he  decides  to  stay  with  an  ugly  young  man  who  is\nfavorite  with  girls.  He  goes  to  his  tipi  and  stays  with  him  many  nights,  asking  him\nwhy  it  is  that  girls  seem  so  fond  of  him.  Ugly  young  man  tells  him  he  got  his  power\nfrom  antelope,  and  he,  being  requested,  takes  him  to  river  that  he  may  obtain  this\npower. He  is  then  left  for  four  days,  seeing  fire  and  water\neach  night.  On  fourth  night  he  faints  and  finds  himself  in  animals'  lodge. His  father  and  mother  die  of  old  age  and  he\nbecomes  leading  medicine-man,  also  dying  of  old  age  after  being  father  of  many\nchildren."

Boy  grows  up  to  be  great  medicine-man."

He  is  doctored  by  different  medicine-men,  but  they  fail  to  cure  him.  Boy\nvisits  him,  blows  different  dusts  upon  wound,  and  heals  him.  Boy's  fame  as  medi-\ncine-man goes  through  village.  In  his  do  toring  he  sings  bear  songs,  and  all  know\nthat  he  has  visited  bears. He  goes  with  her  to  buffalo  wallow,  where  she  becomes  buffalo.\nHe  follows  her  until  they  come  to  bulls,  where  he  ties  presents  on  their  horns. Leader\nof  surround  is  chosen.  Many  bulls  are  killed,  cow  being  permitted  to  escape.  As\nbulls  are  skinned,  eagle  feathers  and  native  tobacco  are  found  on  their  heads,  and\nthey  know  that  Howling  Fox  has  been  instrumental  in  bringing  them.  Howling\nFox  is  given  many  presents  and  ponies.  People  kill  buffalo  four  times  and  they\nreturn  to  their  permanent  village.  Howling  Fox  alone  staying  behind. He  wears  gaming  ring  from  cow  on  his\nleft  arm  and  is  owner  of  ring.  He  gives  presents  of  buffalo  robe  and  pony  to  man\nand  teaches  him  ceremony.  Shortly  after,  Howling  Fox  dies,  because,  as  was  said,\nhe  gave  all  his  knowledge  to  another  man."

THE    BUFFALO    MEDICINE    DANCE.\n\nPeople  are  on  buffalo  hunt  and  are  attacked  by  bull,  who  enters  sacred  tipi  and\ntears  it  to  pieces.  Man  is  sent  for  who  understands  spirits  of  buffalo.  In  after-\nnoon dark  clouds  gather,  rainstorm  follows,  and  woman  is  blown  away.  After\nstorm,  people  are  addressed  by  buffalo,  who  tells  them  that  their  sacred  belongings\nshall  be  restored.  Buffalo  disappears.  Again  buffalo  appears  and  invites  some  of\nbuffalo  medicine-men  to  go  with  him  to  buffalo  country.  They  travel  until  they\ncome  to  steep  bank,  where  they  enter  buffalo  lodge,  passing  on  way  through  deep\nwater.  In  lodge  they  find  bear  and  buffalo,  who  perform  feats  of  sleight-of-hand.\nDuring  performance  animals  arise,  snort,  and  downy  feathers  fall  from  their  mouths.\nOne  buffalo  blows  upon  reed  whistle  and  swallows  it,  throwing  up  feathers.  He\ntells  medicine-men  that  he  gives  them  ceremony,  that  they  shall  have  buffalo  skull\nto  which  they  shall  make  offerings,  for  spirit  of  buffalo  will  reside  in  skull,  and  that\nskull  will  inform  them  through  dreams  as  to  what  they  shall  do  in  ceremony.\nPeople  return  to  village  and  perform  ceremony.\n\n95.    THE    WOMAN   AND    BUFFALO    DANCE.\n\nUnmarried  woman  gives  birth  to  child,  and  because  people  are  angry  at  her\nthey  leave  her  behind  when  they  go  on  hunt.  Child  cries,  she  tries  in  vain  to  stop  it,\nstarts  west,  and  on  hill  finds  buffalo  bull,  who  blows  smoke  from  his  mouth  and  gives\nwoman  root  with  which  to  doctor  child.  He  rolls  on  ground  and  robe  appears,  in\nwhich  she  is  told  to  wrap  child.  Bull  blows  and  calls  three  other  bulls.  They  blow\ntheir  breath  upon  child.  Buffalo  cow  comes.  Child  is  placed  by  cow  and  sleeps.\nWhen  it  awakes  it  is  well.  Buffalo  tell  woman  that  root  will  drive  away  wild\nbeasts  and  that  she  is  to  bathe  child.  She  starts  off,  passes  snake,  and  it  dies  on\naccount  of  root.  Man  comes  to  her  lodge  and  offers  to  be  her  husband.  He\nlearns  of  her  power  and  they  return  west  to  thank  buffalo,  and  he  is  taught\nbuffalo  dance.  He  finds  rattle  where  buffalo  rolls  upon  ground,  which  bears  picture\nof  buffalo  skull.  He  is  to  use  it  in  doctoring.  Buffalo  rolls  again  and  makes  whistle,\nfrom  each  end  of  which  hangs  moon-shaped  shell.  In  doctoring,  man  is  to  blow\nwhistle,  whereupon  he  will  see  bull's  shadow.  If  shadow  does  not  appear,  patient\nis  to  die.  When  boy  grows  up  he  becomes  great  medicine-man  and  is  taught\nbuffalo  dance.\n\n96.   THE    BUFFALO   MEDICINE    DANCE.\n\nBoy  meets  old  buffalo  on  hill  who  tells  him  that  he  is  getting  old.  Buffalo  takes\npity  on  boy  while  boy  feeds  him.  He  hands  boy  little  ball  from  his  stomach,  which,\nwhen  he  smells  it,  will  enable  him  to  see  buffalo.  He  gives  him  whistle  and  some\nroots  which  he  is  to  use  in  doctoring.  In  buffalo  dance  he  is  to  chew  piece  of  ball,\neat  of  root,  and  paint  his  face  with  mud  from  buffalo  wallow  and  eat  piece  of  it,\nwhereupon  he  will  have  buffalo  spirit  and  people  will  give  him  many  presents.  He\ngives  him  power  to  heal  wounds,  but  not  sickness.  Boy  returns  and  tells  his  father\nof  his  adventure;  they  return  to  buffalo,  which  is  now  dead.  Then,  as  he  has  been\ndirected  by  buffalo,  he  cuts  off  its  tail  and  piece  of  scalp.  In  next  medicine-lodge,\nboy  dances  buffalo  dance,  using  robe,  which  changes  its  color.\n\nS30  THE  pawnee:   mythology.\n\n97.    THE  BUFFALO  GAME  MEDICINE."

In  his  sleep  man  appears  to  him  and  tells  him  to\nmake  gaming  sets  up  as  he  has  seen,  that  he  is  to  play  game  on  west  side  of  village,\nfor  there  is  home  of  buffalo.  He  is  not  to  play  in  east,  for  it  is  home  of  diseases,  nor\nin  south,  for  it  is  home  of  dead,  nor  in  north,  for  from  that  direction  enemies  come.\nHe  is  to  make  ash  bow  and  dogwood  arrows.  With  them  he  is  to  kill  two  buffalo\nbulls,  using  their  hides  for  wrapping  for  two  javelins.  In  selecting  wood  for  his\njavelins  he  is  to  darken  his  enemy's  visage  by  cutting  on  north  side,  he  is  to  fight\ndisease  by  cutting  on  east  side,  he  is  to  ward  off  death  by  cutting  on  south  side,  and\nthen  to  cut  tree  down  on  west  side.  Thus  the  leaves  of  tree  will  be  preserved.  He\nis  to  smoke  to  heavens  to  remind  them  that  they  gave  him  game.  Wood  for  second\njavelin  is  to  be  obtained  in  same  way.  Sticks  are  to  be  length  of  his  body  and  they\nare  to  represent  men.  He  is  to  obtain  two  other  sticks  shorter  than  first  two,  and\nthey  are  to  represent  one-horned  buffalo  in  west.  Sticks  are  to  be  spliced  in  pairs.\nHe  is  to  kill  buffalo  cow,  placing  her  head  toward  east,  so  that  buffalo  will  follow  him,\nand  remove  skin  from  about  vulva  with  which  he  is  to  make  ring.  He  then  takes\ngaming  sticks,  representing  at  one  end  ears  and  single  horn.  Two  cross  sticks  are\ntied  on  to  represent  legs;  front  stick  representing  sun,  and  hind  one,  moon,  for  they\nwere  first  to  play  game  in  heavens,  moon  winning  and  giving  sticks  to  men.  After\nsticks  are  prepared  one  is  charred  black  to  represent  darkness,  night,  or  north;  other\nis  left  white  to  represent  light,  day,  or  south.  Next,  he  prepares  ring,  to  which  he\nties  white  bead,  representing  star  which  gave  him  game. In  playing,\nthey  are  to  count  one  hundred  and  twenty,  or  number  of  fingers  and  toes  on  six\nindividuals,  value  of  count  being  determined  by  relation  of  ring  to  different  parts  of\njavelin.  Losing  side  is  to  furnish  fire  in  which  to  boil  meat  for  offering.  At  end  of\ngame  pieces  of  heart  and  tongue  are  offered  to  sun,  moon,  and  stars,  and  game  and\nplayer  is  rubbed  with  fat. In  doctoring,  should  sick  person  have  played  with  sticks,  he  is  to  go  to\ngaming  ground  and  take  dust  from  center  of  ring  where  it  has  stopped  and  let  sick\nperson  smell  of  it  and  then  rub  it  over  his  body.  Other  men  make  gaming  sets  in\nimitation  of  this  one.  Owner  with  black  javelin  in  medicine-lodge  uses  it  as  pipe-\nstem,  although  javelin  is  not  perforated.\n\n98.     LOST  WARRIOR  AND  THE  SINGING  BUFFALO  MEDICINE.\n\nWarriors  are  taken  by  enemy.  One  hides,  and  in  returning  home  loses  his  way.\nHe  cries  to  spirits. THE   BUFFALO  MEDICINE  WAR  SHIELD.\n\nMan  on  hill  is  envious,  seeing  that  boy  is  talking  with  girls,  for  girls  have  refused\nto  talk  with  him.  He  cries  on  second  hill  farther  away  from  village,  and  then\nwanders  off  and  remains  all  winter.  He  returns  in  spring  and  does  not  enter  village,\nfor  he  has  no  home.  He  sets  out  after  herd  of  buffalo,  seeing  among  them  woman.\nHe  asks  her  to  marry  him.  He  goes  with  her  to  buffalo  village  and  woman's  uncle\ntells  him  that  he  wants  presents  of  scalp  and  blue  beads.  Boy  returns  to  his  village,\nenters  chief's  tipi,  obtains  presents,  and  offers  them  to  buffalo.  They  are  thankful\nand  give  boy  shield,  which  he  is  to  wear  upon  his  left  shoulder.  Boy  returns  with\nhis  wife  to  his  village.  It  is  attacked  by  enemy.  He  uses  his  shield  in  battle  and\nkills  many.  He  shows  greater  bravery  in  second  and  third  attacks  upon  village.\nOn  fourth  attack  in  his  excitement  he  wears  his  shield  on  his  right  shoulder.  He  is\nwounded  and  taken  home  to  die.  In  night  buffalo  bull  makes  water  in  front  of  his\ntipi.  In  morning  boy  rubs  some  of  mud  over  his  face  and  returns  and  lies  down,\nwhereupon  many  buffalo  roll  about  in  his  tipi.  Great  dust  appears.  Boy  rolls  in\ndust  again  and  becomes  man  with  buffalo  robe  on  his  shoulder.  He  is  known  there-\nafter as  wonderful  man.  Buffalo  warn  him  never  to  put  buffalo  horn  or  hoof  in\nfire.  Long  time  after,  careless  person,  not  knowing  of  restriction,  throws  spoon  into\nfire  in  his  tipi  and  man  dies.\n\n100.  THE  MAN  WHO  MARRIED  A  DEER.\n\nYoung  man  on  hunt  goes  to  Pahuk,  where  he  associates  with  woman  who  turns\ninto  deer.  Angry  because  he  has  been  deceived,  he  shoots  at  deer  several  times,  but\ncan  not  kill  it.  He  follows  deer  to  swamp,  where  it  becomes  woman.  They  lie\ntogether,  and  both  become  deer  and  wander  over  country,  and  woman  gives  birth  to\ntwo  fawns.  In  meantime  she  teaches  him  deer  power.  He  is  now  able  to  transform\nhimself  into  deer  or  back  into  man  at  his  will.  She  takes  him  to  his  people  and  he\nenters  medicine- lodge  and  asks  permission  to  perform.  When  they  give  it  he  returns\nto  his  wife,  and  she  and  two  fawns  turn  into  human  beings.  They  enter  village,  but\nodor  of  people  is  offensive.  Man  and  his  wife  and  child  enter  medicine-lodge.\nThey  borrow  pair  of  deer  antlers,  sing,  man  places  antlers  on  his  head  and  he  becomes\ndeer.  Next,  he  puts  fawn  skin  over  his  boy  and  boy  turns  into  fawn.  Then  he\ntiims  fawn  into  boy.  At  end  of  performance  medicine-men  acknowledge  his  great\npower  and  make  him  their  leader.  They  live  with  people  many  years.  Woman\ntells  her  husband  that  she  must  now  leave  him.  She  becomes  black-tailed  deer  and\nruns  off.  Man  is  unhappy.  His  children  grow  up  and  both  marry,  his  boy  possess-\ning great  power.  When  man  sees  that  his  children  are  happy,  he  goes  into  timber\nand  never  returns.\n\n101.    THE    DEER    DANCE.\n\nMan  wanders  away  from  village  to  mountains,  and  on  hill  in  dream  sees  black-\npainted  man  standing  by  him  wearing  buffalo  robe.  He  tells  him  he  is  errand\nman  of  deer  society,  and  that  he  is  to  take  him  to  their  lodge.  Man  looks\naround  and  sees  no  one,  but  in  sky  sees  Raven,  who  has  been  speaking  to  him.\nRaven  directs  him  to  top  of  mountains,  where  he  hears  great  noise.  At  entrance  of\nlodge  man  addresses  him  and  tells  him  it  is  he  who  has  spoken  to  him  in  vision,  and\nthat  he  had  become  raven,  and  as  man  seems  afraid  to  go  to  animals'  lodge  he  has\n\n532  THE  pawnee:  mythology.\n\ncaused  many  ravens  to  make  noise  like  human  beings.  They  enter  lodge,  where  man\nfinds  many  animals,  elks  being  leaders.  They  sing,  and  all  have  turned  into  people,\neach  after  his  kind.  They  dance  and  sing,  and  eat  red  beans,  some  of  which  they\ngive  to  man,  who  becomes  very  ill.  He  believes  himself  dead  and  visits  heavens\nand  sees  Tirawa  sitting  in  earth-lodge  holding  bow  in  his  left  hand  and  sage  in  his\nright.  Tirawa  puts  wild  sage  on  ground,  moves  it,  and  red  beans  appear.  Tirawa\ntells  him  he  is  to  return  to  his  people  and  teach  them  this  dance.  At  daylight  people\nturn  into  animals  and  birds  and  leave  lodge.  They  return  each  night  for  four  nights,\nand  man  returns  to  his  people.  On  his  way  home  he  makes  songs  commemorating\nhis  introduction  to  lodge,  and  he  institutes  deer  dance.\n\n102.   THE    WOLF   WARRIOR."

Wolf  asks  man  to  spend  night  with  him,  for\nit  is  to  be  his  last.  As  sun  appears  in  morning  wolf  dies,  crying  with  his  last  breath  to\nsun,  whereupon  man,  as  directed,  cuts  around  wolf's  nose  and  strip  down  his  back,\nwhich  he  is  to  wear  on  his  scalp-lock,  thus  keeping  with  him  spirit  of  wolf,  which  will\nenable  him  to  live  to  old  age.  After  taking  skin  from  wolf,  man  returns  home,  where\nhe  has  been  regarded  as  lost.  He  is  often  absent  from  village.  He  disguises  himself\nand  accompanies  victorious  war  party,  but  claims  no  credit.  In  fall  he  again  joins\nwar  party. He  scouts  again  and  reports  having  seen  Cheyenne  and  Arapaho.\nHe  captures  many  ponies,  which  he  gives  to  leader. They  bum  grass  as  signal  of  their  victorious  approach,  and  paint  their\nfaces  with  charred  grass.  Wolf  Man  becomes  famous  as  warrior,  and  thereafter  is\nleading  scout.  Famous  leader  rides  war  party  into  Mexico.  Wolf  Man  and  com-\npanion are  leading  scouts.  They  seem  never  to  tire.  They  discuss  their  power,\nWolf  Man  explaining  how  he  received  his  from  wolf,  while  other  man  gives  him  root\nwhich  he  uses  as  relief  from  fatigue.  This  be  obtained  from  horse  in  dream.  These\ntwo  travel  incredible  distances  each  day.  They  return  home  successful  and  they\nbecome  close  friends.  Wolf  Man  dies  of  old  age,  his  last  moment  coming  as  ray  of\nsunlight  rests  on  him,  and  thus  he  dies  as  wolf  has  died.\n\n103.    THE    COYOTE  AND   WOLF  MEDICINE.\n\nMan  meets  Coyote,  who  offers  him  his  pipe.  After  he  has  smoked.  Coyote  takes\nhim  to  his  people,  where  he  meets  wolves  and  coyotes.  There  Coyote  introduces\nman  as  his  brother.  Coyotes  roll  in  dust  and  give  him  root  which  will  cure  hydro-\nphobia. They  give  him  other  medicines  for  urinary  troubles.  Next,  wolves  roll  in\ndust  and  give  man  whistle,  blowing  of  which  will  cure  sickness.  Another  Coyote\ngives  him  bone  with  which  to  kill  people.  Coyote  gives  him  bone  for  war  club.\nAnother  Coyote  gives  him  piece  of  his  skull,  which  he  is  to  place  on  his  forehead  to\nprevent  people  from  bewitching  him.  He  returns  home,  blowing  on  his  whistle  on\nway  as  directed.     Animals  hear  him.     He  becomes  medicine-man."

He  is  necessarily  abandoned,  his  friends  giving  him  food  and\ndrink.  In  night  woman  addresses  him,  telling  him  that  she  has  only  done  it  to\nscare  him. He  thinks  he  hears  his  parents\ncalling  him,  but  is  warned  by  Scalped-Man  not  to  try  to  escape. Finally  they  all  land  and  husband  is  instructed  to  have  his  wife  sleep  each\nnight  in  bed  of  cactus,  which  by  morning  has  caused  her  nerves  to  assume  normal\ncondition. In  night  boy  is  told  that  it  is  Breath  or  Wind  who  has\nassisted  him,  and  that  he  is  to  obey  his  wife.  He  goes  on  war-path,  carrying  his\nrattle.  Near  enemy  he  removes  handle,  particles  of  dust  fly  out  from  rattle  and\nbecome  armed  warriors.  They  attack  village,  killing  many  and  capturing  ponies.\nHe  holds  rattle  up  and  warriors  enter,  becoming  dust.  He  becomes  famous  warrior,\nalways  traveling  alone.  Women  desire  to  marry  him.  He  takes  second  wife.  His\nfirst  wife  tells  him  that  he  must  remember  her  and  must  be  kind  to  her.  Once  in\nvisiting  his  second  wife  he  becomes  angry  and  speaks  in  slighting  terms  of  his  first\nwife.  When  he  returns  to  his  first  wife  he  finds  her  bones  upon  bed.  They  are\nplaced  in  grave,  where  he  mourns,  but  no  spirit  addresses  him.  He  institutes  whistle\ndance,  teaches  people  how  to  bewitch,  and  teaches  power  of  bewitching  by  throw-\ning red  beans  into  air.\n\n114.    HANDSOME-BOY.\n\nBoy  is  carefully  guarded  and  well  clothed  by  his  parents  and  is  called  Hand-\nsome-Boy.
